results.question: What do you build?
results.speech: I build applied AI and agentic graph systems. My main projects are GridSeak, a local structural graph of a repository that an agent can query instead of guessing, and GridSchool, a residency where I review each step of a student's route until a company hires them. I also keep this site, which answers only from notes I wrote.

results.question: Why does graph engineering matter if AI can already read a repo?
results.speech: Reading a repo and understanding its structure are different things. A model can read files, but by default it cannot tell which hidden edge will break at runtime or which files sit in the blast radius of a refactor. My view is that understanding code through its graph is becoming more valuable than generating code. A graph lets an agent pull in only the relevant slice, the function, its callers, its callees, and the modules it couples to, so it spends its effort on the change instead of rediscovering the codebase. I also keep track of how strong each piece of evidence is, so a string match never gets treated as a proven dependency.

results.question: What is GridSeak?
results.speech: GridSeak is my open source code graph tool. I describe it as a structural MRI for a repository. It builds a local, deterministic graph of how the code fits together from tree-sitter parses, grep, and the language server, so an agent or engineer can ask what calls a function or what changing a file reaches, and get an answer from the graph instead of a guess. You can find it on my GitHub.

results.question: What are evidence tiers in GridSeak?
results.speech: Evidence tiers are how GridSeak labels where each structural claim comes from. An edge from a tree-sitter parse, an edge found by grep, and an edge confirmed by the language server each carry different weight, and the tool keeps them separate. A grep match is a lead, while a language server confirmation is much closer to proof. I think flattening those into one confident statement is a mistake, so the tier is always shown.

results.question: What is GridSchool and who is it for?
results.speech: GridSchool is the engineering residency I run through my company, GRID SCHOOL LLC. Each student gets an eight week route built around the job they want, and I, a working engineer, review every step until a company hires them. It is for engineers who want a specific next role and a clear path to it, starting from wherever they stand today.

results.question: How long is the GridSchool residency?
results.speech: The current GridSchool residency runs 8 weeks of teaching and review, at 10 to 15 hours a week. After week 8, the weekly one-on-one keeps going until a company hires the student. The price and start dates are covered on a call, which you can book from the GridSchool site.

results.question: How do you check what an agent did?
results.speech: I read the diff the agent produced, run the tests, and then ask what else the change touched that the agent never mentioned. I also want the agent to report which evidence backs each claim, like a grep result confirmed by the language server, rather than telling me a story about the code. A change should be checkable by a person before it's trusted.

results.question: What's the difference between a junior using an agent and an excellent engineer using one?
results.speech: The difference is what happens after the output. A junior takes the agent's change at face value, while an excellent engineer asks whether it was verified, what it missed, and what a structural view of the code would have shown before spending the tokens. For me that review loop after the output is where the value is.

results.question: Tell me about the job search engine you built for students.
results.speech: I built the Hire engine for GridSchool students. It takes the busywork out of a job search so their time goes into preparing, talking to people, and doing the work. Each student gets a daily run ordered by evidence, starting with prep, then referrals found in their own LinkedIn connections export, then profile work, follow-ups, and fresh roles. It prepares role packs for specific applications, and a browser extension fills in forms but never submits on its own. Nothing automates LinkedIn, and a human approves anything that leaves the system.

results.question: What does your AI appointment setter do?
results.speech: The AI setter is an appointment-setting agent I built for GridSchool. When someone answers one of our ads, it replies in chat, answers their questions about the residency, and books a call with me right inside the conversation. If my calendar is unreachable, it sends a booking link instead of failing, so the lead always has a way to book. It also won't quote our price or promise a job.

results.question: How does the map builder plan a route for each student?
results.speech: The map builder drafts a custom route for each student. It works from a library of modules, picks and orders them based on the student's goal, background, and current evidence, and I review the draft before the student sees it. When something changes, like a rejection or a new target company, it redrafts the route from the same library so the plan follows the student.

results.question: What are you weakest at?
results.speech: My main weakness is over-abstracting. I have built general architecture before I had a buyer or a second use case. I correct for it now by shipping the narrow version first and waiting for a real second case before I generalize. A second one is that I have worked alone for a long stretch, so I have had less day-to-day code review than I want, which is one reason I am keen on a strong team. I also used to write long explanations when short ones would do.

results.question: What mistakes have you made building GridSchool?
results.speech: Quite a few, and I keep them written down so I catch them early. The biggest ones: I built general architecture before I had a second use case, so the abstraction cost more than it saved. I built the architecture before I had a buyer. Early GridSchool copy was a long philosophy essay that gave readers nothing to check. I also let language models write in my voice without a corpus, which produced confident paragraphs I would never sign. And I spent a long time on the 12-month residency and the shared multiplayer world, which I have since archived for an 8-week route with weekly 1:1s.

results.question: What kind of roles are you looking for?
results.speech: I am looking for applied AI engineer, agentic systems engineer, developer tooling engineer, and founding engineer roles at an early company. The common thread is building AI systems whose output a team can check before trusting it. I have built retrieval, tool calling, structured output, evals, and cost controls in production at GridSchool and on this site.

results.question: What's your tech stack?
results.speech: My main language is TypeScript, and most of what I ship runs on it, on the server and in the browser. I also write Python, mostly for data work and analysis. For the web I use Astro, React where a page needs real interactivity, and Three.js for the 3D avatar on this site. I deploy on Cloudflare Workers, use Zod for schemas at the boundaries, and work with Postgres for data. For AI work I use LLM APIs like Claude and OpenAI, with structured output, tool calling, retrieval, and evals. Some of my other professional languages are still unfilled in my notes, so I will not list those.

results.question: How do you keep a RAG system from making things up?
results.speech: I keep it from making things up mainly with three rules working together. The model answers only from sources I retrieve, it has to cite those sources, and it refuses when the sources do not cover the question. I test the refusal path as carefully as the answer path, because a confident guess when nothing was found is worse than no system at all. Retrieval starts with lexical search like BM25 because I can see exactly why a chunk matched.

results.question: How does this site keep the model cost bounded?
results.speech: Cost is bounded in a few ways. Each visit gets five live questions to AI Aden. After that the site switches to a free notes-only mode that answers without a model. There is also a daily dollar ceiling on model spend, and every answer shows what it cost, so you can see it too.

results.question: How much does GridSchool cost?
results.speech: I do not publish GridSchool's price on this site, and I cannot quote it here. It is covered on a call, so if you book one from gridschool.org, we can go through it properly.

results.question: Do you guarantee I'll get a job?
results.speech: No, I do not guarantee a job, and GridSchool does not promise one or a placement rate. A company's yes is still theirs to give. What I do offer is review of every step until a company hires you, and a week-2 exit: if either side says it is the wrong room by the end of week 2, the unused tuition comes back. I will not sell a job-or-refund promise, because it pushes both sides toward gaming the outcome.

results.question: What salary are you looking for?
results.speech: I discuss salary directly on a call, so I do not want to name a number here without context. My expectations depend on the role, the level, equity, and whether the job is remote. If you tell me the role you have in mind, I can talk through the range and the shape of the package. You can also book a call or leave me a message.

results.speech: I have not filled in my total years of experience or my earlier employers in these notes yet, so I cannot give you exact figures. My resume has the exact dates and employers, and you can leave me a message if you want me to follow up with them directly.
